fetched_contents.text: Foundry Sand - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. 2 Foundry sand Foundry sand is high quality silica sand that is a by-product from the production of both ferrous and non-ferrous metal casting industries. It is used for the centuries as a moulding casting material because of its high thermal conductivity. For various foundry operations, raw sand is used and several binders and additives are added into it to enhance its properties. Based on binder system used, foundry sand is classified into two categories i.e. clay-bonded (green) sand and chemically bonded sand. As evident from the names, clay-bonded or green sand consists of clay as binder whereas in chemically bonded sand chemicals are used as binders. Green foundry sand is generally composed of 85–95% silica sand, 4–10% of bentonite clay as binder then 2–10% of carbonaceous additive, to improve finishing of casting surface. It also contains traces of oxides such as MgO, K2O, TiO2. Whereas, chemically bonded sand or chemical foundry sand, consists of 93–99% silica sand and about 1–3% chemical binder [5]. The silica sand and chemicals are thoroughly mixed and then a catalyst initiates the reaction that cures and hardens the mould mass. Most commonly used chemical binder are- epoxy resins, sodium silicates, furyl alcohol, phenolic urethanes etc. Presence of carbonaceous additives imparts black colour to green foundry sand whereas chemical foundry sand is light in colour. Green foundry sand is preferred for moulding operations whereas chemical foundry sand is used for both mould making and core making operations, which require higher strengths to withstand the heat of molten metal. Read full article URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0950061817318111 4.13 Foundry sand Foundry sand is a by-product of the ferrous and nonferrous metal casting industry. In this sector, sand has been used for hundreds of years as a molding material due to its thermal conductivity. The sands are successfully recycled and reused several times in a foundry until they reach a limit and are disposed of and referred to as foundry sands. Foundry sand is high-quality silica sand with uniform physical characteristics, which is being used as a fine aggregate substitute in construction applications and as kiln feed in the manufacture of Portland cement. 4.13.1 Physical and mechanical properties Based on ASTM C33-03 recommendations, foundry sands can be used as a substitute for fine aggregates in Portland cement pastes. The American Foundry Society (AFS) has studied foundry sand as a substitute for fine aggregate in concrete (FIRST, 2004). However, foundry sands are generally too fine to allow full substitution. More specifically, between 5% and 12% of the spent foundry sands are smaller than 0.075 mm. Therefore, to meet the specifications of the standard it is necessary to discard part of the fines or to blend the foundry sands with coarse sand. Another characteristic of this material is its content of organic impurities, which can vary widely, reaching very high levels. This can affect its use in applications, such as Portland cement concrete aggregate, in which the control of these elements is important (MOEE, 1993). fetched_contents.text: Chemically-Bonded Sand Casting: Techniques & Products Developed through the 20th Century, chemical-bonded, or resin-bonded, sand casting refers to casting processes that utilise chemically-bonded sand moulds and cores, instead of the clay-bonded systems used in green sand casting. Chemical-bonded moulding systems fall into two basic categories: self-hardening (also known as no bake, self-set or cold-set) and triggered-hardening. The latter includes both heat-activated and gas-triggered systems. Heat-activated systems saw much development in the mid-20th Century, when a number of processes were developed that replaced older oil-bonded methods. By the mid-1970s, however, the gas-triggered cold-box system was firmly establishing itself as a faster and less environmentally-burdensome process for core and mould making. Since then, self-hardening and cold gas-triggered systems have taken an ever-expanding share of the chemical-bonded sand casting market. Pre-hardening the moulds and cores ahead casting allows the production of dimensionally precise castings, compared to green sand casting, where the mould it hardened during casting. These hardened moulds and cores can be automatically assembled on continuous conveyor lines to be cast. In this way, highly complex components can be cast. Once assembled, moulds can either be bottom-filled with the molten metal, to eliminate oxide inclusions and reduce running system turbulence, or via direct top pouring. * Self-hardening mixescomprise sand, a binder and a hardening chemical. The latter two components react and slowly begin to harden as the sand is formed into the mould or core. The hardening continues until the sufficient strength has been gained for casting. * Triggered-hardening systems involve pre-forming the sand-binder mix to the requisite pattern in a core box, and then applying heat or a catalytic gas to activate the hardening process. Once activated, hardening occurs quickly. Within these general categories, however, there are a various techniques available. Development efforts to improve binding systems, particularly to control and reduce the release of harmful gases during mould production and casting, as well as to improve sand reclamation rates, is also ongoing. Furane-based binding systems Developed as far back as the 1950s, furane-based no-bake systems use a furane resin with an acidic hardening chemical. Furan-bonded moulds have good hot strength and erosion resistance, and are relatively easy to reclaim. The curing speed is also easy to control via the percentage and strength of the acid used. On a more challenging note, however, formaldehyde – the subject of tightening regulation in some regions, notably the EU – is released from the mixed sand. When sulphonic acids are used as the hardening agent, sulphur dioxide gas is also released when the mould is cast. Modern furane moulding systems are designed to counter the challenge posed by hazardous emissions. ESHANOL and FUROTEC furane binders from Foseco, for example, have been formulated for very low emissions during application and pouring. Both also offer very high binding characteristics to ensure the lower possible additions (<1%) are required to product good-quality moulds and cores. Meanwhile, CATASET acidic catalysts are also designed for minimum addition rates, as well as for optimisable bench life and curing time to foundry requirements. Urethane-based binding systems A patent for a phenolic-urethane binder system was first filed in 1978 by Ashland Oil Inc., in the US. More expensive than furan binders, urethane binder systems traditionally come in three parts, comprising a phenolic-urethane resin, an isocyanate (e.g., methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, MDI), and a liquid amine catalyst; two-part systems are also now available. Originally urethane binders were based on aromatic organic solvents, which resulted in very high fume emissions on mixing and the release of an acrid smoke during casting. However, low-odour polyurethane cold-set binders have now been developed, such as POLISET from Foseco, extending the market for urethane-binding systems: * POLISET AL is a two-component binder system developed for aluminium casting that utilizes non-aromatic solvents and low-phenol and -formaldehyde binders to deliver rapid strength development, as well as excellent post-casting breakdown. * POLISET E is a three-component phenolic binder system, suitable for both ferrous and non-ferrous casting applications, that offers flexible set times (2 – 30 minutes) and excellent hot strength (low erosion defects and good dimensional accuracy). Ester-hardened alkaline phenolic moulding systems Ester-hardened alkaline phenolic resins were developed in the late 1970s and early 1980s (e.g., this patent, filed by Borden UK Ltd in 1982), but began to gain in prominence at the turn of the Millennium when more focus was placed on developing safer and more environmentally-friendly binder systems. Modern systems, such as FENOTEC from Foseco, comprise a water-soluble alkaline phenolic resin with a range of liquid organic ester activation agents, and combine good stripping and casting finish with low fume emissions during mixing, casting and knockout. FENOTEC is a flexible binding solution, being suitable for both mould and core production, casting of a wide range of alloys, and with a range of sands (silica, chromite, zircon and olivine: for more on the different sand types, see our discussion of green sand moulding). It may also be used as a gas-triggered system in which the ester is added as a vapour and blown through the sand-resin mix. Green clay-bonded foundry sand is a conventional, recyclable system built on silica sand with a clay binder and water, plus carbonaceous additives. The main ingredients and their approximate mass fractions are clearly summarized in the evidence: green foundry sand is generally composed of 85–95% silica sand, 4–10% bentonite clay as binder, then 2–10% carbonaceous additive, with traces of oxides such as MgO, K₂O, TiO₂ [N1-F1]. Additional sources confirm the same general structure: green sand consists of high-quality silica sand, about 5–10% bentonite clay, 2 to 5% water, and about 5% sea coal or similar carbonaceous additive [N1-R3]. A practical DIY guideline also supports a 90% sand–10% binder ratio as a rough starting point, indicating that the sand is the dominant component and the binder is kept relatively low by weight [N3-R3].

The role of the clay binder is to provide green strength and cohesion. Bentonite clay acts as the primary binder in green sand, and its function is to hold the sand particles together into a coherent mixture that can be compacted into a mold. The evidence explicitly states that bentonite clay is the binder in green foundry sand, and that the mix is typically kept at about 5–10% bentonite [N1-R3]. The green strength comes from the clay’s ability to adsorb water and form a cohesive network between sand grains, which allows the sand to resist collapse during handling and mold preparation [N1-F1]. Water is also a key component, with the evidence showing 2 to 5% water in green sand [N1-R3], though the exact amount can vary depending on the sand quality and the desired workability.

Common additives serve specific purposes in the mix. The most prominent additive is the carbonaceous material, such as sea coal, which is present at about 5% in one source [N1-R3]. Its purpose is to improve finishing of the casting surface, as indicated in the ScienceDirect overview [N1-F1]. Other sources suggest that additives may be used to control moisture, permeability, and surface finish, and that bentonite ratios can be adjusted to reduce excess binder [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These additives are therefore not the main load-bearing component but rather functional ingredients that enhance moldability, surface quality, and the overall casting performance of the green sand system.

Overall, the composition is dominated by silica sand (85–95%), with the binder and additives forming a much smaller proportion by weight. The system is intended for molding operations, where green strength and reusability are important, and the carbonaceous additive helps achieve a better casting finish [N1-F1][N3-R3].

Chemically bonded foundry sand differs fundamentally from green clay-bonded sand in its binder system: instead of bentonite clay, it uses a chemical binder such as phenolic-urethane resin, furan resin, or other resin-based systems. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand or chemical foundry sand consists of 93–99% silica sand and about 1–3% chemical binder [N1-F1]. A more detailed source on chemical-bonded sand casting describes resin-bonded systems and notes that sand, binder, and hardening chemical are the core components in self-hardening mixes [N2-F2]. The evidence also explicitly lists phenolic-urethane resin systems as a common type, with the binder traditionally coming in three parts: phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate (e.g., methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, MDI), and a liquid amine catalyst [N2-R1]. Another source notes that urethane binder systems can be two-part or three-part, with POLISET E being a three-component phenolic binder system suitable for ferrous and non-ferrous casting [N2-F2].

The role of the resin and binder in curing and strength development is central to chemically bonded sand. In a phenolic-urethane system, the bonding process mechanism involves a polyaddition reaction between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. This is consistent with the broader description of resin-bonded sand, which emphasizes that the resin and binder system are the basis of the casting process [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern, then heat or a catalytic gas is applied to activate the hardening process [N2-F2]. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is formed into the mold, continuing to harden until sufficient strength is achieved [N2-F2]. This means that strength development is chemical and curing-driven, rather than water-dependent.

Common additives and how they affect performance are also evident in the evidence. The main additive in chemically bonded sand is the hardening chemical or catalyst, which initiates the curing reaction [N2-F2]. The evidence also indicates that catalytic gases may be used in gas-triggered systems, and that the choice of catalyst can affect bench life, curing time, and casting performance [N2-F2]. In phenolic-urethane systems, the hardening chemical is often an acidic component, and the curing speed can be controlled by the percentage and strength of the acid used [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that the choice of binder type can affect emissions, release of harmful gases, and sand reclamation rates, with modern systems designed to reduce these issues [N2-F2]. Additives such as catalysts, gases, and acid hardeners are therefore not merely incidental; they are essential for controlling the curing behavior and dimensional stability of the chemically bonded sand.

In summary, chemically bonded foundry sand is primarily silica sand (93–99%) plus a small chemical binder (1–3%) and associated curing additives. The resin and binder system provide curing and strength development through chemical reaction, while the curing conditions and additives determine the process type and performance characteristics [N1-F1][N2-F2].

The comparison between green and chemically bonded sands shows clear differences in moisture content and curing requirements. Green sand is inherently moisture-dependent because it relies on water to activate the clay binder and provide workability [N1-F1][N3-R3]. The evidence states that green sand typically contains 2 to 5% water, while chemically bonded sand is described as requiring a curing chemical rather than water [N1-R3][N2-F2]. For chemically bonded systems, the curing process is either triggered by heat, gas, or chemical activation, and the hardening chemical or catalyst is the key driver of strength development [N2-F2]. This means that the curing requirement for chemically bonded sand is chemical and process-dependent, whereas green sand is water-dependent and more manual in operation.

Differences in green strength, reusability, and dimensional stability are also notable. Green sand is preferred for molding operations because it is easier to handle and reuse, and it can be reclaimed and reused multiple times [N1-R2][N3-R1]. However, green sand is generally less dimensionally stable than chemically bonded sand because it relies on a clay binder that can be affected by moisture, compaction, and subsequent casting heat [N1-F1]. In contrast, chemically bonded sand is used for both mold making and core making, and the evidence emphasizes that these systems can produce dimensionally precise castings because the molds are pre-hardened before casting [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal, implying better dimensional stability under thermal load [N1-F1]. The comparison source further states that chemically bonded sand casting yields smoother surfaces and finer details, and that dimensional accuracy improves with the process [N5-F4].

Tradeoffs in cost, environmental impact, and casting performance are evident. Green sand is described as cost-efficient and environmentally friendly because it is recyclable, reusable, and requires minimal investment in equipment and materials [N5-F4]. However, chemically bonded sand is generally more expensive than green sand, and some sources indicate that resin-bonded systems may involve more complex materials and higher costs [N2-F2]. Environmental impact is also a tradeoff: chemically bonded systems can produce harmful gases such as formaldehyde or sulphur dioxide, but modern systems are designed to reduce emissions [N2-F2]. On the casting performance side, chemically bonded sand is superior for complex geometries, thin-walled components, and high-precision applications, while green sand remains the go-to choice for simple and cost-sensitive operations [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence suggests that green sand offers lower cost and better recyclability, while chemically bonded sand offers better dimensional control, surface finish, and strength, at the expense of higher cost and more complex handling [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

The chemistry and curing of chemically bonded sand are defined by the resin and binder system, which is usually a polyaddition or polyurethane-based reaction. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a polyaddition reaction between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. It also notes that in phenolic-urethane systems, the resin is composed of a phenolic-urethane resin, an isocyanate (e.g., methylene diphenyl diisocyanate, MDI), and a liquid amine catalyst [N2-R1]. Another source describes urethane binder systems as coming in three parts and explains that the reaction produces a sand coating that provides sufficient bonding strength to enable pattern removal with enough bonded sand strength [N7-R3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that the binder chemistry is not merely a simple adhesive but a multi-component system that forms a chemically cross-linked network during curing.

Curing conditions differ sharply from green sand. In chemically bonded sand, the curing can be either self-hardening or triggered-hardening. Self-hardening mixes are formed into the mold and then harden slowly as the sand is shaped; triggered-hardening systems, in contrast, require heat, gas, or catalytic activation to start the curing process [N2-F2]. The evidence also mentions that the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern, then heat or catalytic gas is applied to activate the hardening process [N2-F2]. This is important because it shows that chemically bonded sand is not cured by moisture alone, as green sand is. Instead, it is cured by chemical activation, with the hardening chemical or catalyst being the initiating agent [N2-F2].

The effects of binder chemistry on dimensional stability are significant. The evidence notes that chemically bonded sand can produce dimensionally precise castings because the molds are pre-hardened before casting [N2-F2]. It also implies that the binder chemistry affects dimensional stability through its curing behavior and the resulting microstructure of the sand system [N2-F2]. The evidence further states that the choice of binder type can affect emissions, release of harmful gases, and sand reclamation rates, and that modern systems are designed to improve dimensional accuracy and reduce emissions [N2-F2]. This suggests that the binder chemistry is not only responsible for strength and hardness but also for maintaining consistent dimensions and improving process control.

In short, the resin and binder system in chemically bonded sand work through a polyaddition or polyurethane reaction, and the curing conditions are chemical-activation driven rather than water-dependent. This chemistry contributes to dimensional stability, while also shaping the curing process and environmental profile of the system [N2-R4][N2-R1][N2-F2].

## Final integrated comparison of green clay-bonded and chemically bonded foundry sands

Green clay-bonded foundry sands and chemically bonded foundry sands are two fundamentally different systems, distinguished by their binder chemistry, curing behavior, and composition. Green sands rely on bentonite clay and water, while chemically bonded sands use resin-based binders and chemical curing agents. The evidence consistently supports this distinction and gives a clear way to compare the two systems in terms of composition, strength, reusability, dimensional stability, and process tradeoffs.

### 1. Main ingredients and approximate mass fractions

**Green clay-bonded sands** are dominated by silica sand, with bentonite clay and water plus carbonaceous additives forming the remaining components. The most direct evidence states that green foundry sand is generally composed of **85–95% silica sand**, **4–10% bentonite clay** as binder, and then **2–10% carbonaceous additive** [N1-F1]. A second source supports this general structure, noting that green sand consists of **high-quality silica sand**, about **5–10% bentonite clay**, **2 to 5% water**, and about **5% sea coal or similar carbonaceous additive** [N1-R3]. A practical guideline also suggests a rough 90% sand–10% binder ratio as a starting point [N3-R3].

**Chemically bonded sands**, by contrast, are almost entirely silica sand with a much smaller chemical binder. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand or chemical foundry sand consists of **93–99% silica sand** and about **1–3% chemical binder** [N1-F1]. A more detailed source on chemical-bonded sand casting emphasizes that the system is built around **sand, binder, and hardening chemical** [N2-F2]. Phenolic-urethane systems are also explicitly listed as a common type, with the binder traditionally coming in three parts: **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1].

So, in terms of composition ratios, the difference is stark: green sands are **sand-heavy** with a moderate binder, while chemically bonded sands are **sand-heavy** but with a very small, specialized chemical binder and associated curing agents [N1-F1][N2-F2].

### 2. Role of the binder and how it contributes to green strength

In green clay-bonded sands, the **bentonite clay** acts as the primary binder. Its role is to hold the sand particles together and provide cohesion so the sand can be compacted into a mold. The evidence explicitly states that bentonite clay is the binder in green foundry sand [N1-R3], and that the system is kept at about **5–10% bentonite** [N1-R3]. Water is also a key component, present at about **2 to 5%** in green sand [N1-R3], and it helps activate the clay and improve workability.

The green strength in this system comes from the clay’s ability to adsorb water and form a cohesive network between sand grains. This cohesion is what gives green sand its characteristic handling properties and allows it to be reused multiple times [N1-R2][N3-R1]. The carbonaceous additive, such as sea coal, is present to improve casting surface finish [N1-R3][N1-F1].

In chemically bonded sands, the role of the binder is different. Rather than clay, the binder is a **chemical resin system** such as phenolic-urethane, furan, or other resin-based binder. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. Another source notes that phenolic-urethane systems consist of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. This means the binder in chemically bonded sand is not simply a clay adhesive; it is a **multi-component chemical system** that crosslinks during curing [N2-R1][N2-R4].

The **resin and binder system** in chemically bonded sands is what provides the strength and hardness needed before casting. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is formed into the mold, continuing to harden until sufficient strength is achieved [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, heat, gas, or catalytic activation is used to start the curing process [N2-F2]. This is a major difference from green sand, where strength is water-dependent and curing is handled manually.

### 3. Common additives and their purpose in the mix

In green clay-bonded sands, the main additive is the **carbonaceous material**, such as sea coal or similar additive, which is present at about **5%** in one source [N1-R3]. Its purpose is to improve the **finishing of the casting surface** [N1-F1]. Other sources suggest that additives may be used to control **moisture, permeability, and surface finish**, and that bentonite ratios can be adjusted to reduce excess binder [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These additives are therefore functional ingredients that support moldability and surface quality rather than being the main structural component.

In chemically bonded sands, the main additive is the **hardening chemical or catalyst**. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand requires a curing chemical rather than water, and that the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern, then heat, gas, or catalytic activation is applied to start the curing process [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that the choice of catalyst can affect **bench life, curing time, and casting performance** [N2-F2]. In phenolic-urethane systems, the hardening chemical is often an acidic component, and the curing speed can be controlled by the percentage and strength of the acid used [N2-F2]. Modern systems are also designed to reduce emissions, release of harmful gases, and improve reclamation rates [N2-F2]. So, the additives in chemically bonded sand are not just incidental; they are essential for controlling the curing behavior and dimensional stability.

### 4. Reaction mechanism of resin and binder system

The chemistry of chemically bonded sands is centered on a **polyaddition or polyurethane-type reaction**. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. It also notes that phenolic-urethane systems are composed of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. Another source explains that urethane binder systems can be three parts and that the reaction produces a **sand coating** that provides enough bonding strength for pattern removal [N7-R3].

Taken together, these sources show that the binder chemistry is a **multi-component reaction system** rather than a simple adhesive. The resin and binder form a **chemically cross-linked network** during curing, which is what gives chemically bonded sand its strength and dimensional stability [N2-R4][N2-R1][N7-R3].

### 5. Curing conditions and how they differ from green sand

Curing conditions are one of the clearest differences between the two systems.

- **Green sand** is **moisture-dependent**. It relies on water to activate the clay binder and provide workability [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The curing process is essentially manual: the sand is mixed with water, compacted, and then cast while still wet [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Chemically bonded sand**, by contrast, is **curing-dependent**. It requires a **hardening chemical, heat, gas, or catalytic activation** to start the curing process [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern and then activated by heat or catalytic gas [N2-F2]. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is shaped into the mold [N2-F2]. This means that chemically bonded sand is cured by **chemical activation** rather than by water alone [N2-F2].

This difference has important implications for process control. Green sand is simpler to handle and reuse, but chemically bonded sand can be pre-hardened before casting, allowing for **greater dimensional control** and more consistent performance [N2-F2].

### 6. Effects of binder chemistry on dimensional stability

The evidence indicates that binder chemistry has a major impact on **dimensional stability**. Chemically bonded sand is used for both mold making and core making because it can produce **dimensionally precise castings** [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that chemically bonded sand casting yields **smoother surfaces and finer details**, and that **dimensional accuracy improves** with the process [N5-F4]. This is because the binder chemistry and curing conditions help maintain consistent dimensions and reduce distortion.

In green sand, dimensional stability is generally less predictable. The evidence notes that green sand is preferred for molding operations, but that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal [N1-F1]. This implies that green sand is less dimensionally stable under thermal load compared to chemically bonded sand [N1-F1][N5-F4].

### 7. Differences in moisture content and curing requirements

Moisture content and curing requirements are central to the comparison.

- **Green sand** has a **water content** of about **2 to 5%** [N1-R3]. It is moisture-dependent, and its curing is handled manually with water and binder [N1-F1][N3-R3].
- **Chemically bonded sand** does **not** rely on water for curing. Instead, it relies on a **curing chemical, heat, gas, or catalytic activation** [N2-F2]. The evidence explicitly states that chemically bonded sand is cured by the hardening chemical rather than water [N2-F2].

This is a key practical distinction: green sand is easier to handle in terms of moisture management, while chemically bonded sand requires more precise control of curing chemistry and process conditions [N2-F2][N5-F4].

### 8. Differences in green strength, reusability, and dimensional stability

**Green strength:** Green sand has **green strength** from the clay binder and water, which gives it enough cohesion to be compacted into a mold [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, however, has a different kind of green strength: it is **pre-hardened strength** from the resin and binder system [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal [N1-F1].

**Reusability:** Green sand is **highly reusable** and recyclable, and the evidence emphasizes that green sand is **recyclable and reusable**, making it cost-efficient and environmentally friendly [N1-R2][N5-F4]. In contrast, chemically bonded sand is more difficult to reclaim than green sand [N2-F2]. Modern systems are designed to improve reclamation rates, but the evidence still indicates that reclaiming chemically bonded sand is more challenging than in green sand casting [N2-F2].

**Dimensional stability:** Green sand is generally less dimensionally stable than chemically bonded sand. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand can produce dimensionally precise castings and that the molds are pre-hardened before casting [N2-F2]. It also implies that green sand can be affected by moisture, compaction, and casting heat, which can reduce dimensional consistency [N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is better suited to high-precision applications and thin-walled components [N5-F4].

### 9. Tradeoffs in cost, environmental impact, and casting performance

The evidence identifies several tradeoffs between the two systems.

- **Cost:** Green sand is described as **cost-efficient** and requiring **minimal investment in equipment and materials** [N5-F4]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is generally **more expensive** than green sand [N2-F2]. Some sources indicate that resin-bonded systems may involve more complex materials and higher costs [N2-F2].
- **Environmental impact:** Green sand is **recyclable** and **reusable**, making it a more environmentally friendly option [N1-R2][N5-F4]. Chemically bonded sand, however, can produce **harmful gases** such as formaldehyde or sulphur dioxide, depending on the binder system [N2-F2]. Modern systems are designed to reduce emissions, but this still introduces an environmental tradeoff [N2-F2].
- **Casting performance:** Chemically bonded sand is superior for **complex geometries, thin-walled components, and high-precision applications** because it can produce smoother surfaces and finer details [N5-F4]. Green sand remains the go-to choice for **simple and cost-sensitive operations** because it is easier to handle and reuse [N5-F4].

### 10. Summary

In summary, **green clay-bonded foundry sand** and **chemically bonded foundry sand** differ in several key ways:

| Feature                     | Green Clay-Bonded Sand                             | Chemically Bonded Sand                               |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Main ingredient**        | Silica sand (85–95%)                               | Silica sand (93–99%)                                 |
| **Binder**                 | Bentonite clay (4–10%)                             | Chemical binder (1–3%)                                |
| **Curing mechanism**       | Water-dependent, manual curing                     | Chemical activation, heat/gas/catalytic curing        |
| **Green strength**         | Provided by clay and water                         | Provided by resin and binder system                   |
| **Moisture content**       | About 2 to 5%                                      | Not water-dependent; cured by chemical agents         |
| **Dimensional stability**  | Generally less stable                               | More dimensionally stable and precise                 |
| **Reusability**            | Highly reusable and recyclable                      | More difficult to reclaim; modern systems improve this |
| **Cost**                   | Lower cost                                         | Higher cost                                          |
| **Environmental impact**   | More environmentally friendly                       | Can produce harmful emissions; modern systems reduce this |
| **Casting performance**    | Good for simple, cost-sensitive operations         | Better for complex, thin-walled, high-precision work  |

### Bottom line

If you want the simplest answer: **green sand is simple and reusable, while chemically bonded sand is stronger and more precise but more expensive and more chemically complex** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. For a deep-research answer, the key synthesis is that the two systems differ by **binder chemistry, curing mechanism, moisture dependence, dimensional stability, reusability, cost, and environmental impact**, with green sands being the conventional, recyclable option and chemically bonded sands being the more advanced, precision-oriented alternative [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

### 2. Role of the binder and how it contributes to green strength

In green clay-bonded sands, the **bentonite clay** acts as the primary binder. Its role is to hold the sand particles together and provide cohesion so the sand can be compacted into a mold. The evidence explicitly states that bentonite clay is the binder in green foundry sand [N1-R3], and that the system is kept at about **5–10% bentonite** [N1-R3]. Water is also a key component, present at about **2 to 5%** in green sand [N1-R3], and it helps activate the clay and improve workability.

The green strength in this system comes from the clay’s ability to adsorb water and form a cohesive network between sand grains. This cohesion is what gives green sand its characteristic handling properties and allows it to be reused multiple times [N1-R2][N3-R1]. The carbonaceous additive, such as sea coal, is present to improve casting surface finish [N1-R3][N1-F1].

In chemically bonded sands, the role of the binder is different. Rather than clay, the binder is a **chemical resin system** such as phenolic-urethane, furan, or other resin-based binder. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. Another source notes that phenolic-urethane systems consist of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. This means the binder in chemically bonded sand is not simply a clay adhesive; it is a **multi-component chemical system** that crosslinks during curing [N2-R1][N2-R4].

The **resin and binder system** in chemically bonded sands is what provides the strength and hardness needed before casting. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is formed into the mold, continuing to harden until sufficient strength is achieved [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, heat, gas, or catalytic activation is used to start the curing process [N2-F2]. This is a major difference from green sand, where strength is water-dependent and curing is handled manually.

### 3. Common additives and their purpose in the mix

In green clay-bonded sands, the main additive is the **carbonaceous material**, such as sea coal or similar additive, which is present at about **5%** in one source [N1-R3]. Its purpose is to improve the **finishing of the casting surface** [N1-F1]. Other sources suggest that additives may be used to control **moisture, permeability, and surface finish**, and that bentonite ratios can be adjusted to reduce excess binder [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These additives are therefore functional ingredients that support moldability and surface quality rather than being the main structural component.

In chemically bonded sands, the main additive is the **hardening chemical or catalyst**. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand requires a curing chemical rather than water, and that the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern, then heat, gas, or catalytic activation is applied to start the curing process [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that the choice of catalyst can affect **bench life, curing time, and casting performance** [N2-F2]. In phenolic-urethane systems, the hardening chemical is often an acidic component, and the curing speed can be controlled by the percentage and strength of the acid used [N2-F2]. Modern systems are also designed to reduce emissions, release of harmful gases, and improve reclamation rates [N2-F2]. So, the additives in chemically bonded sand are not just incidental; they are essential for controlling the curing behavior and dimensional stability.

### 4. Reaction mechanism of resin and binder system

The chemistry of chemically bonded sands is centered on a **polyaddition or polyurethane-type reaction**. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. It also notes that phenolic-urethane systems are composed of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. Another source explains that urethane binder systems can be three parts and that the reaction produces a **sand coating** that provides enough bonding strength for pattern removal [N7-R3].

Taken together, these sources show that the binder chemistry is a **multi-component reaction system** rather than a simple adhesive. The resin and binder form a **chemically cross-linked network** during curing, which is what gives chemically bonded sand its strength and dimensional stability [N2-R4][N2-R1][N7-R3].

### 5. Curing conditions and how they differ from green sand

Curing conditions are one of the clearest differences between the two systems.

- **Chemically bonded sand**, by contrast, is **curing-dependent**. It requires a **hardening chemical, heat, gas, or catalytic activation** to start the curing process [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern and then activated by heat or catalytic gas [N2-F2]. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is shaped into the mold [N2-F2]. This means that chemically bonded sand is cured by **chemical activation** rather than by water alone [N2-F2].

This difference has important implications for process control. Green sand is simpler to handle and reuse, but chemically bonded sand can be pre-hardened before casting, allowing for **greater dimensional control** and more consistent performance [N2-F2].

The evidence indicates that binder chemistry has a major impact on **dimensional stability**. Chemically bonded sand is used for both mold making and core making because it can produce **dimensionally precise castings** [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that chemically bonded sand casting yields **smoother surfaces and finer details**, and that **dimensional accuracy improves** with the process [N5-F4]. This is because the binder chemistry and curing conditions help maintain consistent dimensions and reduce distortion.

This is a key practical distinction: green sand is easier to handle in terms of moisture management, while chemically bonded sand requires more precise control of curing chemistry and process conditions [N2-F2][N5-F4].

**Green strength:** Green sand has **green strength** from the clay binder and water, which gives it enough cohesion to be compacted into a mold [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, however, has a different kind of green strength: it is **pre-hardened strength** from the resin and binder system [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal [N1-F1].

**Reusability:** Green sand is **highly reusable** and recyclable, and the evidence emphasizes that green sand is **recyclable and reusable**, making it cost-efficient and environmentally friendly [N1-R2][N5-F4]. Modern systems are designed to improve reclamation rates, but the evidence still indicates that reclaiming chemically bonded sand is more challenging than in green sand casting [N2-F2].

**Dimensional stability:** Green sand is generally less dimensionally stable than chemically bonded sand. It also implies that green sand can be affected by moisture, compaction, and casting heat, which can reduce dimensional consistency [N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is better suited to high-precision applications and thin-walled components [N5-F4].

### 9. Tradeoffs in cost, environmental impact, and casting performance

The evidence identifies several tradeoffs between the two systems.

- **Cost:** Green sand is described as **cost-efficient** and requiring **minimal investment in equipment and materials** [N5-F4]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is generally **more expensive** than green sand [N2-F2]. Some sources indicate that resin-bonded systems may involve more complex materials and higher costs [N2-F2].
- **Environmental impact:** Green sand is **recyclable** and **reusable**, making it a more environmentally friendly option [N1-R2][N5-F4]. Modern systems are designed to reduce emissions, but this still introduces an environmental tradeoff [N2-F2].
- **Casting performance:** Chemically bonded sand is superior for **complex geometries, thin-walled components, and high-precision applications** because it can produce smoother surfaces and finer details [N5-F4]. Green sand remains the go-to choice for **simple and cost-sensitive operations** because it is easier to handle and reuse [N5-F4].

### 10. Summary

| Feature                     | Green Clay-Bonded Sand                             | Chemically Bonded Sand                               |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Main ingredient**        | Silica sand (85–95%)                               | Silica sand (93–99%)                                 |
| **Binder**                 | Bentonite clay (4–10%)                             | Chemical binder (1–3%)                                |

| **Dimensional stability**  | Generally less stable                               | More dimensionally stable and precise                 |

| **Cost**                   | Lower cost                                         | Higher cost                                          |
| **Environmental impact**   | More environmentally friendly                       | Can produce harmful emissions; modern systems reduce this |
| **Casting performance**    | Good for simple, cost-sensitive operations         | Better for complex, thin-walled, high-precision work  |

### Bottom line

If you want the simplest answer: **green sand is simple and reusable, while chemically bonded sand is stronger and more precise but more expensive and more chemically complex** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. A practical guideline also suggests a rough 90% sand–10% binder ratio as a starting point [N3-R3].

**Chemically bonded sands**, by contrast, are almost entirely silica sand with a much smaller chemical binder. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand or chemical foundry sand consists of **93–99% silica sand** and about **1–3% chemical binder** [N1-F1]. A more detailed source on chemical-bonded sand casting emphasizes that the system is built around **sand, binder, and hardening chemical** [N2-F2]. Phenolic-urethane systems are also explicitly listed as a common type, with the binder traditionally coming in three parts: **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1].

The green strength in this system comes from the clay’s ability to adsorb water and form a cohesive network between sand grains. This cohesion is what gives green sand its characteristic handling properties and allows it to be reused multiple times [N1-R2][N3-R1]. **Green strength:** Green sand has **green strength** from the clay binder and water, which gives it enough cohesion to be compacted into a mold [N1-R3][N1-F1]. ### 10. Summary

In summary, **green clay-bonded foundry sand** and **chemically bonded foundry sand** differ in several key ways:

| Feature                     | Green Clay-Bonded Sand                             | Chemically Bonded Sand                               |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Main ingredient**        | Silica sand (85–95%)                               | Silica sand (93–99%)                                 |

### Bottom line

If you want the simplest answer: **green sand is simple and reusable, while chemically bonded sand is stronger and more precise but more expensive and more chemically complex** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. Another source notes that phenolic-urethane systems consist of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. This means the binder in chemically bonded sand is not simply a clay adhesive; it is a **multi-component chemical system** that crosslinks during curing [N2-R1][N2-R4].

The **resin and binder system** in chemically bonded sands is what provides the strength and hardness needed before casting. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is formed into the mold, continuing to harden until sufficient strength is achieved [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, heat, gas, or catalytic activation is used to start the curing process [N2-F2]. This is a major difference from green sand, where strength is water-dependent and curing is handled manually.

### 3. Common additives and their purpose in the mix

In green clay-bonded sands, the main additive is the **carbonaceous material**, such as sea coal or similar additive, which is present at about **5%** in one source [N1-R3]. Its purpose is to improve the **finishing of the casting surface** [N1-F1]. Other sources suggest that additives may be used to control **moisture, permeability, and surface finish**, and that bentonite ratios can be adjusted to reduce excess binder [N3-R3][N3-R4]. These additives are therefore functional ingredients that support moldability and surface quality rather than being the main structural component.

In chemically bonded sands, the main additive is the **hardening chemical or catalyst**. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand requires a curing chemical rather than water, and that the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern, then heat, gas, or catalytic activation is applied to start the curing process [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that the choice of catalyst can affect **bench life, curing time, and casting performance** [N2-F2]. In phenolic-urethane systems, the hardening chemical is often an acidic component, and the curing speed can be controlled by the percentage and strength of the acid used [N2-F2]. Modern systems are also designed to reduce emissions, release of harmful gases, and improve reclamation rates [N2-F2]. So, the additives in chemically bonded sand are not just incidental; they are essential for controlling the curing behavior and dimensional stability.

### 4. Reaction mechanism of resin and binder system

The chemistry of chemically bonded sands is centered on a **polyaddition or polyurethane-type reaction**. The evidence states that the bonding process mechanism involves a **polyaddition reaction** between a phenolic resin (polyol component) and isocyanate components [N2-R4]. It also notes that phenolic-urethane systems are composed of **phenolic-urethane resin, isocyanate, and a liquid amine catalyst** [N2-R1]. Another source explains that urethane binder systems can be three parts and that the reaction produces a **sand coating** that provides enough bonding strength for pattern removal [N7-R3].

Taken together, these sources show that the binder chemistry is a **multi-component reaction system** rather than a simple adhesive. The resin and binder form a **chemically cross-linked network** during curing, which is what gives chemically bonded sand its strength and dimensional stability [N2-R4][N2-R1][N7-R3].

### 5. Curing conditions and how they differ from green sand

Curing conditions are one of the clearest differences between the two systems.

- **Green sand** is **moisture-dependent**. It relies on water to activate the clay binder and provide workability [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The curing process is essentially manual: the sand is mixed with water, compacted, and then cast while still wet [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Chemically bonded sand**, by contrast, is **curing-dependent**. It requires a **hardening chemical, heat, gas, or catalytic activation** to start the curing process [N2-F2]. In triggered-hardening systems, the sand-binder mix is formed into the pattern and then activated by heat or catalytic gas [N2-F2]. In self-hardening systems, the resin and hardening chemical react slowly as the sand is shaped into the mold [N2-F2]. This means that chemically bonded sand is cured by **chemical activation** rather than by water alone [N2-F2].

This difference has important implications for process control. Green sand is simpler to handle and reuse, but chemically bonded sand can be pre-hardened before casting, allowing for **greater dimensional control** and more consistent performance [N2-F2].

### 6. Effects of binder chemistry on dimensional stability

The evidence indicates that binder chemistry has a major impact on **dimensional stability**. Chemically bonded sand is used for both mold making and core making because it can produce **dimensionally precise castings** [N1-F1]. The evidence also states that chemically bonded sand casting yields **smoother surfaces and finer details**, and that **dimensional accuracy improves** with the process [N5-F4]. This is because the binder chemistry and curing conditions help maintain consistent dimensions and reduce distortion.

In green sand, dimensional stability is generally less predictable. The evidence notes that green sand is preferred for molding operations, but that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal [N1-F1]. This implies that green sand is less dimensionally stable under thermal load compared to chemically bonded sand [N1-F1][N5-F4].

### 7. Differences in moisture content and curing requirements

Moisture content and curing requirements are central to the comparison.

- **Green sand** has a **water content** of about **2 to 5%** [N1-R3]. It is moisture-dependent, and its curing is handled manually with water and binder [N1-F1][N3-R3].
- **Chemically bonded sand** does **not** rely on water for curing. Instead, it relies on a **curing chemical, heat, gas, or catalytic activation** [N2-F2]. The evidence explicitly states that chemically bonded sand is cured by the hardening chemical rather than water [N2-F2].

This is a key practical distinction: green sand is easier to handle in terms of moisture management, while chemically bonded sand requires more precise control of curing chemistry and process conditions [N2-F2][N5-F4].

### 8. Differences in green strength, reusability, and dimensional stability

**Green strength:** Green sand has **green strength** from the clay binder and water, which gives it enough cohesion to be compacted into a mold [N1-R3][N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, however, has a different kind of green strength: it is **pre-hardened strength** from the resin and binder system [N2-F2]. The evidence also notes that chemically bonded sand is used where higher strength is required to withstand the heat of molten metal [N1-F1].

**Reusability:** Green sand is **highly reusable** and recyclable, and the evidence emphasizes that green sand is **recyclable and reusable**, making it cost-efficient and environmentally friendly [N1-R2][N5-F4]. In contrast, chemically bonded sand is more difficult to reclaim than green sand [N2-F2]. Modern systems are designed to improve reclamation rates, but the evidence still indicates that reclaiming chemically bonded sand is more challenging than in green sand casting [N2-F2].

**Dimensional stability:** Green sand is generally less dimensionally stable than chemically bonded sand. The evidence states that chemically bonded sand can produce dimensionally precise castings and that the molds are pre-hardened before casting [N2-F2]. It also implies that green sand can be affected by moisture, compaction, and casting heat, which can reduce dimensional consistency [N1-F1]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is better suited to high-precision applications and thin-walled components [N5-F4].

### 9. Tradeoffs in cost, environmental impact, and casting performance

The evidence identifies several tradeoffs between the two systems.

- **Cost:** Green sand is described as **cost-efficient** and requiring **minimal investment in equipment and materials** [N5-F4]. Chemically bonded sand, by contrast, is generally **more expensive** than green sand [N2-F2]. Some sources indicate that resin-bonded systems may involve more complex materials and higher costs [N2-F2].
- **Environmental impact:** Green sand is **recyclable** and **reusable**, making it a more environmentally friendly option [N1-R2][N5-F4]. Chemically bonded sand, however, can produce **harmful gases** such as formaldehyde or sulphur dioxide, depending on the binder system [N2-F2]. Modern systems are designed to reduce emissions, but this still introduces an environmental tradeoff [N2-F2].
- **Casting performance:** Chemically bonded sand is superior for **complex geometries, thin-walled components, and high-precision applications** because it can produce smoother surfaces and finer details [N5-F4]. Green sand remains the go-to choice for **simple and cost-sensitive operations** because it is easier to handle and reuse [N5-F4].

### 10. Summary

In summary, **green clay-bonded foundry sand** and **chemically bonded foundry sand** differ in several key ways:

| Feature                     | Green Clay-Bonded Sand                             | Chemically Bonded Sand                               |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
| **Main ingredient**        | Silica sand (85–95%)                               | Silica sand (93–99%)                                 |
| **Binder**                 | Bentonite clay (4–10%)                             | Chemical binder (1–3%)                                |
| **Curing mechanism**       | Water-dependent, manual curing                     | Chemical activation, heat/gas/catalytic curing        |
| **Green strength**         | Provided by clay and water                         | Provided by resin and binder system                   |
| **Moisture content**       | About 2 to 5%                                      | Not water-dependent; cured by chemical agents         |
| **Dimensional stability**  | Generally less stable                               | More dimensionally stable and precise                 |
| **Reusability**            | Highly reusable and recyclable                      | More difficult to reclaim; modern systems improve this |
| **Cost**                   | Lower cost                                         | Higher cost                                          |
| **Environmental impact**   | More environmentally friendly                       | Can produce harmful emissions; modern systems reduce this |
| **Casting performance**    | Good for simple, cost-sensitive operations         | Better for complex, thin-walled, high-precision work  |

### Bottom line

If you want the simplest answer: **green sand is simple and reusable, while chemically bonded sand is stronger and more precise but more expensive and more chemically complex** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4]. For a deep-research answer, the key synthesis is that the two systems differ by **binder chemistry, curing mechanism, moisture dependence, dimensional stability, reusability, cost, and environmental impact**, with green sands being the conventional, recyclable option and chemically bonded sands being the more advanced, precision-oriented alternative [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].
